title: Trump: Paul Manafort to Trump: Add me to your campaign. I'll work for free.
description_short: Trump: Paul Manafort to Trump: Add me to your campaign. I'll work for free.
description_medium: Paul Manafort reportedly offered to join Donald Trump’s campaign without pay. The offer marks a step in Manafort’s entry into the campaign, but it does not settle when their relationship began.
description_long:
Paul Manafort reportedly offered to work for Donald Trump’s campaign without pay, an episode tied to his later role as campaign chairman. A critique of the New York Times account disputes its suggestion that the men first became close in 2016, citing comments from Manafort spokesperson Jason Maloni. Manafort later served as Trump’s campaign chairman.

The reported offer and their relationship timeline are separate claims. Even if Manafort made the offer, it does not prove that 2016 was their first contact. The date, wording and circumstances of the proposal remain unsettled.

title: Donald Trump breaks the law asking Russia to find more Clinton emails
description_short: Donald Trump breaks the law asking Russia to find more Clinton emails
description_medium: During the 2016 campaign, Donald Trump publicly urged Russia to find Hillary Clinton’s missing emails, saying, “Russia, if you’re listening, I hope you’re able to find the 30,000 emails that are missing.” The remark drew concern because it invited a foreign government to seek information about his opponent. Whether the statement violated a specific law is a separate legal question.
description_long:
In July 2016, Donald Trump addressed Russia at a campaign news conference and urged it to locate emails Hillary Clinton had deleted from her private server. He said, “Russia, if you’re listening, I hope you’re able to find the 30,000 emails that are missing.” The appeal drew attention because it asked a foreign government to seek material damaging to Trump’s opponent during the presidential race.

The public statement and the legal label in the headline are different questions. The quote documents what Trump asked for; a legal conclusion requires identifying a statute and establishing its elements.

title: National Fiscal Collapse and Default - $36.1 Trillion Debt Crisis and Economic Destruction
description_short: National Fiscal Collapse and Default - $36.1 Trillion Debt Crisis and Economic Destruction
description_medium: Federal fiscal concern centers on rising debt-service costs and the possibility of a debt-ceiling crisis. A Peterson Foundation article describes interest burdens and the risk of missed payments if Congress fails to act. A separate Center for American Progress analysis models a hypothetical repeat financial crisis under Project 2025 proposals that could limit regulators’ response. These are risk scenarios; the United States did not default on $36.1 trillion as claimed.
description_long:
The Peter G. Peterson Foundation’s debt-crisis article, written during the 2023 budget debate, warned that rising interest costs were making federal debt harder to manage. It cited $33.6 trillion in debt and $879 billion in fiscal year 2023 interest costs, and described a debt-ceiling standoff as a risk of missed payments. That was a warning about fiscal strain, not a report of a default. A separate Center for American Progress analysis examines a different risk: it argues that Project 2025 could weaken financial regulation and limit the Federal Reserve’s lender-of-last-resort role. It estimates losses under a hypothetical repeat of the 2007–08 financial crisis.

The United States did not default on its federal debt in 2025. The recession, three million lost jobs, $130,000 mortgage-cost increase and $850 billion debt rise described in the original claim cannot be presented as consequences of that alleged default. The claims that the dollar lost its reserve-currency status and that a crisis caused these harms remain unsubstantiated. The issue is how fiscal and regulatory choices might affect future risk.
subcategory: National Fiscal Collapse and Economic Destruction
notes: needs_context: the Peterson Foundation article is a 2023 warning about debt and interest costs; the Center for American Progress models a potential repeat financial crisis under Project 2025 proposals. Neither documents an actual U.S. default or the job losses, mortgage costs, debt increase, recession, or reserve-currency loss claimed here.

title: Trump: New York Times editor changes FBI's Russia story to cover for Trump
description_short: Trump: New York Times editor changes FBI's Russia story to cover for Trump
description_medium: The FBI arranged a September 2016 meeting with New York Times reporter Eric Lichtblau while the newspaper was preparing a story about alleged ties between the Trump Organization and a Russian bank. The contact placed federal investigators and journalists working on the same subject in direct communication. The allegation that an editor changed the story to protect Trump remains unverified.
description_long:
In September 2016, the FBI arranged a meeting with New York Times reporter Eric Lichtblau while the newspaper was preparing a story about alleged ties between the Trump Organization and a Russian bank. The bureau had heard from one of Lichtblau’s sources that the Times was reporting on those connections. The meeting brought a federal investigation and journalism about the same subject into contact.

An allegation that a Times editor changed the story to protect Trump concerns an editorial decision, separate from the FBI meeting itself. The meeting alone does not establish that an editor changed the article or why. The episode raises questions about the boundary between law-enforcement inquiries and a newsroom’s handling of politically sensitive reporting.

title: Trump: Benjamin Netanyahu meets with Putin in Moscow, praised by Trump

title: Trump: White nationalist kills 23 people at a Walmart in Texas

title: Trump: After Dark: The Capitol is cleared, Trump says Democrats earned the attack
description_short: Trump: After Dark: The Capitol is cleared, Trump says Democrats earned the attack
description_medium: After rioters stormed the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021, Congress returned under heavy guard to resume counting electoral votes. The attack delayed certification of Joe Biden’s victory for hours and forced lawmakers to leave the chamber. The delay between initial authorization and arrival of National Guard troops became a focus of scrutiny of the response.
description_long:
On January 6, 2021, supporters of President Donald Trump stormed the U.S. Capitol and delayed Congress’s certification of Joe Biden’s election victory for hours. Reuters reported that lawmakers returned to work under heavy guard after the attack. Army authorization to deploy D.C. National Guard troops came before they began arriving at the Capitol later that afternoon.

The delay between authorization and arrival became central to questions about the response. Congress reconvened and completed the electoral count after the Capitol was secured.

title: Trump: Investigation into who sent Hegseth Signalgate texts, potential coverup

The office had spent several weeks interviewing participants. The inquiry concerned who authored the messages; its outcome is not established.
description_long:

The inquiry examined whether the messages were written by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or by members of his staff. Investigators had spent several weeks interviewing participants by the time the matter was reported on June 7, 2025.
